n: Isaiah 14 opens with mercy: the Lord will again choose Israel, settle them in their land, and foreigners will join them. Babylon’s fall makes Israel’s return possible.

f.w: the strangers shall be joined with them

n: Nations will help Israel return from the ends of the earth to their promised lands, and Israel will rule over its former oppressors. The Book of Mormon adds “from far unto the ends of the earth” and “lands of promise,” broadening the gathering.

f.w: they shall return to their lands of promise

n: The Lord will give Israel rest from sorrow, fear, and hard slavery.

f.w: the Lord shall give thee rest

n: Israel will sing a taunt-song over the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has come to an end! The golden city is no more!”

f.g: Here a taunt-song or mocking poem.
Perhaps “the fury” or “the exactress of gold” in Hebrew.

n: The Lord has broken the staff and scepter of wicked rulers.
The tyrant who beat nations without pause and ruled in rage is now hunted himself, and no one stops it.
The whole earth is at rest and bursts into song at his fall.
Even the trees rejoice: since he fell, no woodcutter comes to chop them down. Conquerors stripped Lebanon’s forests for their building projects.

f.w: no feller is come up against us
f.g: No woodcutter comes to cut us down.

n: The underworld (Sheol) stirs to greet him. The ghosts of dead kings rise from their thrones to meet the newcomer.

f.g: Sheol — the world of the dead.

n: They mock him: “You’ve become weak like us!” Death levels the mightiest king.

f.w: Art thou also become weak as we?

n: His splendor and music are buried in the grave; maggots are his bed and worms his blanket.

“How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” The Hebrew helel means “shining one” or “morning star.” While aimed at Babylon’s king, Latter-day Saint scripture applies it to Satan, who fell from heaven through pride.

f.w: O Lucifer, son of the morning
f.g: Latin lucifer, “light-bearer,” translates Hebrew helel ben shachar, “shining one, son of the dawn.”

n: His heart said: “I will climb to heaven, set my throne above God’s stars, and sit on the mount of assembly in the far north” — where ancient peoples imagined the gods met.

f.g: The mountain where the divine council was thought to meet.

n: “I will rise above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.” This is the essence of pride — wanting to replace God.

f.w: I will be like the Most High

n: Instead he will be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.

f.g: The farthest depths of the grave.

n: Onlookers stare and wonder: “Is this the man who shook the earth and kingdoms?”
“Who turned the world into a wasteland, destroyed cities, and never let his prisoners go home?” Satan likewise holds his captives fast.

f.w: opened not the house of his prisoners

n: Other kings lie in honor in their own tombs.
But he is thrown out of his grave like a rejected branch, covered with the slain, a corpse trampled underfoot. Denial of burial was the ultimate disgrace.

f.g: A detested shoot or a rotten branch.

n: He will not share their honorable burial because he ruined his own land and people. The offspring of evildoers will never be famous.
His dynasty must be cut off so it cannot rise again or fill the world with its cities.

f.w: for the iniquities of their fathers

n: The Lord will rise against Babylon and wipe out its name, survivors, and descendants.
Babylon will become a swamp for wild birds, swept away by God’s broom of destruction.

f.g: A marsh bird, or possibly a hedgehog.

n: The Lord swears that what He has planned will surely happen.

f.w: as I have purposed, so shall it stand

n: Isaiah turns back to his own day: God will crush the Assyrian on His mountains and lift Assyria’s yoke from Judah — fulfilled when Sennacherib’s army was destroyed near Jerusalem.

f.w: I will bring the Assyrian in my land

n: This is God’s plan for the whole earth; His hand is stretched out over all nations.

f.w: the hand that is stretched out upon all nations

n: When the Lord of Hosts has planned, who can cancel it? When His hand is stretched out, who can turn it back?
A new oracle, dated to the year King Ahaz died (around 715 BC).
Philistia should not celebrate the death of the king who struck it. From that serpent’s root will come an even deadlier viper — a worse threat to come.
The poorest in Israel will find food and safety, but Philistia will be destroyed by famine and the sword.
Philistia’s gates and cities will wail as an army comes from the north like smoke, with no stragglers in its ranks.

What answer will be given to messengers from other nations? That the Lord has founded Zion, and His poor and humble people will find refuge in it. Isaiah’s chapters quoted by Nephi end on this note of hope.
